You know that we speak of a man, calling him lots of different things, attributing colours to him, and also shapes, dimensions, excellences and vices. In all these cases, and numerous others, we are saying not only that he is a man, but also that he is good, and countless other things. And in other cases, by the same argument, we propose that each is one, and then refer to it as many, and so we describe it by many names.
What you say is true.

Well, at any rate, I believe we have provided a feast for the young and for the old men whose learning came late in their lives. For it is easy for anyone to appreciate quite readily that it is impossible for the many to be one and also for one to be many, and indeed they delight in forbidding man from being called good, and they only allow good to be called good and man to be called man. Indeed, Theaetetus, I imagine you have often met those who take this sort of thing seriously. Sometimes older men who are amazed at such marvels, due to the poverty-stricken state of their intellect, actually believe that they have discovered the very repository of all wisdom.
They certainly do.

Then, so that our discussion may be all inclusive, we should direct our questioning now to all those who have ever discoursed on being in any way at all, and to those with whom we discussed this earlier.
And the questions are?

"Whether we may neither attach being to motion and rest, nor attach anything at all to anything else, and should we therefore propose, in our own discussions, that these are unmixed, and it is impossible for them to participate in one another? Or should we have grouped them all together as the same, in their capacity for communion with one another? Or can some have this capacity while others do not?" Well, Theaetetus, can we say which of these options they would choose?
I cannot answer these questions on their behalf at all.
Then why don't you answer them one by one, and see what the consequences are in each case?
A good suggestion.
First, if you wish, let's propose that they say that nothing has any power of communion with anything else at all. In that case, movement and rest will have no share of being, will they?
Not in that case.
But will either of them be, if they have no communion with being?
They will not.

Well, all parties have been instantly overthrown by this concession it seems, including the 'universe is motion' people, those who say it is one and at rest, and anyone who maintains that things that are consist of forms which are always just the same as they are. Indeed, all of these people associate being with something, some by saying that the universe is actually movement, others by saying that it is actually rest.
Quite so.

And, indeed, those who propose to combine all things at one time and to separate them at some other time, either by having unlimited things coming from one and returning to one, or else by dividing all things into finite elements and making combinations of these, regardless of whether they propose that this happens successively or continuously, these people would be talking nonsense in all cases, if, in fact, there is no comingling.
Correct.
And what's more, the people who pursue this question, in the most ridiculous manner, are those who allow nothing to be referred to as different because it shares a different characteristic.
How?

Well, presumably they are compelled to use 'to be' in relation to everything. They cannot help employing 'apart' and 'the others' and 'itself', and very many more expressions, and connecting them when they speak, and so they are refuting themselves. The enemy and future opponent is within themselves, as the saying goes, and they walk about carrying his voice inside them like the strange ventriloquist, Eurycles.
The comparison you make is both accurate and true.
Well then, should we concede to all things the capacity for intercommunion with one another?
Even I would be able to do away with that suggestion.
How?
Well, movement itself would be totally at rest, while rest itself would, in turn, be moving if they were to come together with one another.
And, presumably, it must be utterly impossible that movement be at rest, and rest in motion?
It must be.
Only the third option is left then.
Yes.
Well, it must be some one of the following: either everything will mix together or nothing will, or some will and others will not.
There are no other options.
And yet the first two were found to be impossible.
Yes.
So anyone who wishes to give the right answer will select the last of the three.
Exactly.

Now, since some things will do this and others will not, they would be behaving much like the letters of the alphabet, for some of them will not fit together with one another, while others will fit together.
Of course.

And the vowels are better at this than the other letters. They are like a bond running through them all so that it is impossible for one of the others to attach to anything else without at least one of the vowels.
Certainly.
Does everyone know what letters can combine with what, or is a skill required by someone who is to do this properly?
There is a skill.
What is it?
Grammar.

And isn't it the same where high and low notes are concerned? Does the musical person have the skill to recognise which notes go together and which do not, while the unmusical person does not understand this?
Yes, it is the same.
And we shall find that similar distinctions between skill and lack of skill apply to other subjects.
Of course.

Yes. And since we have agreed that the kinds can also mix with one another in this same way, mustn't a man who is going to show correctly which of the kinds accord with one another or reject one another proceed through the arguments with some knowledge? And will he also need some knowledge to show whether there are certain kinds which pervade all the kinds and keep them together, so that they can be mixed together, and again, in the case of division, whether the causes of division are entirely different?
How could he do it without knowledge, perhaps even the supreme knowledge?

Well now, Theaetetus, what are we going to call this knowledge? Or, by Zeus, have we stumbled unwittingly upon the knowledge belonging to free men? And is it possible that we have found first the philosopher, whilst looking for the sophist?
What do you mean?
This division on the basis of kinds, without thinking that the same form is a different form or that a different one is the same, should we not say that this belongs to dialectical knowledge?
Yes, we should.

Therefore, someone who can do this readily discerns one characteristic extending entirely through many things, each of which is separate and one; and many characteristics which are different from one another, encompassed externally by one characteristic; furthermore, one characteristic connected in one kind through multiplicities that are wholes; and many characteristics which are distinct and completely separate. This is knowing how to distinguish, kind by kind, which way they commune and which way they do not.
Entirely so.
And I am sure that you will never grant this dialectical skill to anyone except a man who loves wisdom, purely and righteously.
Indeed, how could one grant it to anyone else?

It is in some such place as this that we shall find the philosopher, both now and hereafter, if we search for him. It is, indeed, difficult to see this person plainly, but the difficulty of seeing the sophist is of a different sort from this.
How?
Well, the sophist runs away into the darkness of non-being, attaching himself to this by practice, and he is hard to discern because of the darkness of the place. Is this so?
So it seems.

However the philosopher is always devoted, through reasoning, to the characteristic of what is. And he is also not at all easy to see because of the brightness of that region, as it is impossible for the eyes of the common soul to sustain the gaze that looks towards the divine.
Yes, all this is no less likely to be so than what was said about the sophist.
Well, we shall consider the philosopher in more detail presently, if we so desire. But it is obvious, I presume, that we must not give up on the sophist until we can see him properly.
Very good.

Indeed, we have actually agreed now that some of the kinds will combine with one another, while others will not, and some will combine with few, others with many, and also that some are all-pervasive and are allowed to combine with everything. So we should proceed to the next issue by considering the following question, not about all the forms, lest we get confused by the multiplicity, but selecting some of those which are said to be the most important. We should first ask what sort each is, and then what their power to commune with one another is. In this way, we shall at least understand something about being and non-being, as far as our current method of enquiry allows, even if we cannot apprehend them with total clarity, and we may somehow be allowed to say that 'what is not', is actually non-being, and avoid reproach.
Yes, we must do this.
Now, the most important kinds are those we have just mentioned – being itself, rest and motion.
Very much so.
And we also say that two of them do not mix with one another.
They do not.
And yet being mixes with both, for presumably both are.
Of course.
So there are these three.
Of course.
And of these, each of the two is different from the other, and the same as itself.
Quite so.

Well now, what precisely are the 'same' and the 'different' which we have just mentioned? Are they two additional kinds, apart from the first three, two kinds which must necessarily combine with the three, and should we investigate them as though there were five and not three? Or is this 'same' and 'different' something belonging to the other three, which we are referring to without noticing it?
Perhaps.
But of course, motion and rest are neither different nor the same.
How so?
Whatever we attribute to motion and rest jointly cannot itself be either of the two.
Why is that?

Because motion would then be at rest, and rest would be moving. For the involvement of either of the two with both of them will compel the other one to change to the opposite of its own nature, since it is partaking of its opposite.
Exactly.
However, both partake of the same and the different.
Yes.
Therefore, we may not say that either motion or rest is the same or the different.
No.
Well then, should we think of 'what is' and 'the same' as one thing?
Perhaps.
But if 'what is' and 'the same' do not signify anything different, then saying once more that motion and rest both are will amount to referring to them both as the same.
Yes, but that is impossible.
So it is impossible for 'the same' and 'what is' to be one.
Quite.
Well, should we propose that the same is a fourth form in addition to the other three?
Yes, certainly.
Yes, but should we say that the different is a fifth? Or must we think of the different, and what is, as two names for one kind?
Perhaps.
But I think you concede that some things that are, are always spoken of just by themselves, while some are always spoken of in relation to others.
So they are.
And different is always in relation to another. Is this so?
Just so.

But this would not be the case if what is and different were not utterly distinct. But if different, like what is, were to partake of both relations, some of the different things would sometimes be different, but not in relation to another. But now we find, simply, that whatever is different necessarily turns out to be the very thing it is, namely, different from something else.
It is exactly as you say.
Then we must say that the nature of the different is a fifth form among these forms we are selecting.
Yes.
And we shall say that this pervades all the others, for each one is different from the others, not because of its own nature, but because of participation in the characteristic of different.
Yes, precisely.
Now, let us say the following about these five, taking them up one by one.
What?
First, that motion is completely different from rest. Is this so?
It is so.
So it is not rest.
Not at all.
And yet, because of participation in being, it is.
It is.
Then again, motion is different from the same.
I dare say.
So it is not the same.
No, it is not.
And yet it is the same as itself, because everything partakes of the same.
Yes, indeed.

So we should accept that motion is the same and not the same, without making difficulties. For when we say it is the same and then not the same, we are not speaking in a similar manner. Rather, when we say it is the same, it is because of its participation in the same in relation to itself. And when we say it is not the same, it is because of its communion with different, a communion by which it is separated from the same and becomes not the same but different. So that it is correct, in turn, to say that it is not the same after all.
Yes, certainly.
Yes, and if motion itself were somehow to partake of rest, it would not be strange to say that motion was resting.
And that is perfectly valid, provided we are going to accept that some of the kinds will mix with one another, and some will not.
And, indeed, we arrived at a proof of this before now, establishing that this process is in accordance with nature.
Of course.
Then let's say this once more. Motion is different from the different, just as it was other than the same and rest.
Yes, it must be.
So, in a sense then, it is not different and it is different, according to the current argument.
True.

Then, what about the next point? Shall we say that motion is different from three of the kinds but not from the fourth, though we have agreed that there are five items concerning which, and among which, we propose to conduct our enquiry?
How could we? For we cannot accept that their number is less than what was shown a moment ago.
So, should we persist fearlessly in maintaining that motion is different from being?
Yes, with no fear at all.
Well then, it is clear that motion is actually 'non-being'. And yet it is, since in fact it partakes of being.
Yes, that is perfectly clear.

So, of necessity, what is not is, both in the case of motion and all of the kinds, for in all cases the nature of the different, by rendering each different from what is, makes it what is not. And, indeed, in this way, we are right to say, on the same basis, that all of them are not, and again, because they partake of being, that they are and have being.
Very likely.
So, in the case of each of the forms, 'what is' is many, and 'what is not' is unlimited in multiplicity.
So it seems.
Well then, we must also say that what is, itself, is different from the others.
We must.

And we also found that as many as the others are, to that extent what is, is not. For on the one hand, not being those others it is itself one, and furthermore, it is not, in respect of number, those unlimited others.
Quite so.

Now, we should not make difficulties over these either since the nature of the kinds involves communion with one another. But if anyone does not accept this, he must prevail over our previous arguments and then take on their consequences.
What you propose is very fair.
Well, let us note the following.
What?
When we speak of 'what is not', it seems we are not speaking of something opposite to 'what is', but only of something different.
In what way?
For example, when we say that something is 'not large', are we indicating by this phrase that it is small rather than equal? Is that how it seems to you?
How could it?

So, whenever it is said that a negative signifies an opposite, we shall not accept that. We shall only go so far as to say that prefixing 'not' or 'non' indicates something else apart from the words which follow, or rather, apart from the things to which the words uttered after the negatives may refer.
Entirely so.
Let's think this through as follows, if you agree.
In what way?
It seems to me that the nature of different is broken up in the same way that knowledge is.
How?

Well, presumably knowledge is one, and so is the nature of different, but each portion of knowledge applicable to something in particular has been separated off and given its own particular title. That's why so many skills and branches of knowledge are referred to.
Yes, certainly.
And although the nature of different is one, the same thing happens to the parts.
Very likely, but how should we describe it?
Is there some part of different which contrasts with beauty?
There is.
Now should we say that this is nameless, or does it have a title of its own?
It has. For each time we mention 'non-beauty', this is different from the nature of beauty, and from nothing else.
Come now, tell me this.
What?
On this basis, has non-beauty turned out to be some distinct part of a single kind among things that are, and does it, in turn, stand in contrast to another kind among things that are?
It does.
Then it seems non-beauty turns out to be a contrast of 'what is' with 'what is'.
Quite right.
Well then, based on this account, is beauty more included among things that are, and non-beauty less so?
It is not.
So, should we say, on the same basis, that there is non-largeness and largeness itself?
On the same basis.
And should we therefore place non-justice in the same relation towards justice, in that one is no more than the other is?
Of course.

Well, we shall also describe the others in the same way. Since, in fact, the nature of different has been shown to be included among things that are, and since it is, we must necessarily propose that the parts of it are also things that are, no less.
Yes, we must.

Therefore, it seems, when part of the nature of different, and part of the nature of 'what is' are set against one another, the contrast is no less being than what is, itself, if such a statement is legitimate, and this contrast is not indicating the opposite of 'what is', but only something different from that.
Yes, that is very clear.
So, what should we call this?
Obviously it is 'what is not', the very thing we were seeking because of the sophist.

And does it, as you say, have no less being than anything else? And should we now declare boldly that 'what is not' certainly is, and has its own nature? And just as largeness was large and beauty was beautiful, and the same applied to non-largeness and non-beauty, should we say on the same basis that 'what is not' was and is 'what is not', a single form counted among the many things that are? Do we still have any doubt about this, Theaetetus?
Not at all.
Now, do you realise that we have shown little regard for Parmenides' prohibition?
In what way?
In our previous enquiry, we have forged ahead in our search, and presented the man with something he forbade us to consider.
How?
Well, he says, "For never shall this be proved that things that are not, are, but do thou, in thine enquiry, hold back thy thought from this way."
Yes, that is what he says.

Yet we have shown not only that things that are not, are. We have also revealed the form upon which 'what is not' happens to be based. In fact, having shown that the nature of different is, and is divided up among all things that are in relation to one another, we have dared to maintain that each part of different that contrasts with what is, is really 'what is not'.
Yes, stranger, and the statements we have made seem to me to be entirely true.

Then let no one say that we have dared to maintain that 'what is not' is the opposite of 'what is'. For we long since said farewell to talk of opposite of 'what is', whether there is or is not such a thing, and whether it has an account or is utterly devoid of one. Now, in relation to 'what is not' which we have proposed to be, let someone refute us, and either persuade us that we have not formulated it correctly, or, until he is able to refute it, he must say what we say, that the kinds combine with one another, and 'what is' and the different go through them all, and through one another, and the different, by partaking of 'what is', is, because of that participation, although it is not what it partakes of, but is different. And being different from 'what is', clearly it must be possible for it to be 'what is not'. And, in turn, 'what is', by partaking of the different, will be other from the other kinds, and since it is different from all of them, it is not each of them, nor all of them together except for itself. Consequently, 'what is' undoubtedly is not, in countless instances, and the others, individually and collectively, are in many cases, but are not in many cases.
True.

And one who is at a loss to believe these contradictions must consider these matters for himself and offer a better account than we have just given. But if he has taken hold of something difficult, and finds pleasure now in dragging the arguments to one extreme and now to another, his exertions are not worth taking very seriously, as our current arguments would suggest. For this is neither inventive nor difficult to discover. But what is difficult, and beautiful, is something else.
What is it?

What we said before, allowing such considerations as ineffective; to be able to follow what is said, refuting it stage by stage; if anyone proposes that the different is somehow the same, or the same different, in the very respect in which, and the very way that he says one experiences the other. But by saying that the same is somehow different, and the different is the same, and the great is small, and the like is unlike, and to derive pleasure from constantly bringing forward such oppositions in arguments, this is no real refutation. Indeed, it is obvious that someone who has just appeared on the scene is grasping at a beginning understanding of things that are.
Yes, that is so.
Well now, my friend, the attempt to separate everything from everything else is, in general, an inappropriate response and is, in fact, the activity of someone who is uneducated and unphilosophical.
Why is that?

Yes, this very approach of dissociating each thing from everything else is the total disappearance of all argument. Indeed, the interweaving of forms with one another is the basis from which our discourse arises.
True.
So, consider the timely battle which we waged just now against people like that, and how we have compelled them to allow one to mix with another.
To what end?

So that argument may continue to exist for us. For we would have been deprived of this if we had also deprived ourselves of the interweaving of forms with one another. Indeed, our argument has somehow arisen for us from the interweaving of forms with one another.
True.
Now since we have got rid of this difficulty, but at the same time agreed that being is to be associated with non-being, perhaps we should now try to consider speech.
How so?
If 'what is not' has nothing to do with speech, all argument is necessarily false, while in fact it has been associated with it, and so there is false speech, and false thinking.
Just so.
But if there is falsity, deception arises.
Yes.
And if there is deception, everything is necessarily full of images, likenesses and appearances.
Of course.

And we said that the sophist took refuge in some such place, but he completely denied that there is falsity at all. For he said that 'what is not' could not be thought or stated, since 'what is not' does not partake of being in any way.
Just so.

And now it has appeared that 'what is not' partakes of being, so he probably will not contest the matter further on that basis. Yet he might say that some of the forms partake of 'what is not', while others do not, and speech and opinion are among those which do not. So in opting again for the contention that the skills of image-making and appearance-making, in which we said he was contained, do not exist at all, he might also argue that there is no false opinion or speech. For opinion and speech have no communion with 'what is not'. And in the absence of this association, there is no possibility of any falsity. That's why we must first investigate speech, opinion and appearance, to see precisely what they are, so that, having seen them, we shall recognise their communion with 'what is not', and having recognised this, we shall prove that there is falsity, and having proved this, we shall imprison the sophist there, if we can keep our hold of him, and if we cannot, we shall release him and search in another kind.

Stranger, this expression about the sophist at the outset did indeed appear to be true, that this kind is hard to hunt. For he turns out to be replete with stratagems, and whenever he employs them, he must be vanquished before he can be caught. But now, although he has barely been overcome, he is already objecting that 'what is not', is not. For he is a wonder.
Well, my friend, it is the man with greater experience who will be best able to give the more accurate account, since whoever has been confounded for the longest time, often, is more vexed.
A good point.
Well, let's continue with the present argument and not get vexed.
Why should we?

Indeed, what comes first, in my view, is the question of speech, just as it was earlier in the case of the forms. For this is what we need to consider now: is 'what is not' associated with this too, or is speech entirely true, with no falsity ever arising in this?
Yes, this is what we should consider.
Come now, since we said as much in relation to the forms and letters of the alphabet, let's consider names again in the same way.
Yes, but what should we look for in them?
Whether they all combine with one another, none of them combine, or some can do so, while others cannot.
Well, this is clear in any case: that some can and some cannot.
Perhaps you mean the following: that any words which are uttered in succession and indicate something are combined, while those which are not significant when uttered in succession are not combined.
What you say? Why?
I imagined that you were making the same response that I have actually had in mind. Indeed, we recognise two kinds of vocal expressions about being.
How?
One is referred to as a name, and the other as a verb.
Tell me what each of these is.
The expression that applies to actions, we presumably refer to as a verb.
Yes.
While the vocal label applicable to those who perform such actions is a name.
Quite so.
Well, no statement can ever arise from a string of names that are uttered in succession, or even of verbs separated from names.
I do not understand.
Yes, it was clear when you responded just now that what I am saying is different. For my point was that the sequence does not constitute a statement.
How?
Take for instance "walks, runs, sleeps", and the other verbs which signify actions: even if someone were to recite them all in turn, that would not constitute any statement at all.
Why not?

So again, when "lion, stag, horse" are uttered, and any other names of those who perform actions, this sequence does not constitute a statement either. Indeed, neither in the first case nor in this one are the spoken words associated with any action, or in actuality, of one who acts or does not act. Nor will it ever do so, until someone mixes verbs with names. And as soon as he does so, the joining together produces a statement, the first and the smallest of statements, I dare say.
What do you mean by this?
Whenever someone says, "a man understands", do you say that this is the shortest and the first statement?
I do.

Indeed, it now provides some information about what is, becomes, has become or is to become, and not just naming, but enacting something by combining verbs with names. That is why we have said that it has spoken, and not merely named. And what is more, this combination is the very thing to which we attached the title 'speech'.
Correct.

Now, just as some things fit together with one another, while others do not, the same applies to vocal expressions, some of which do not fit together, while those that do fit together produce statements.
Just so.
But there is still one further consideration.
What?
Whenever there is a statement, it must be a statement about something. Indeed, a statement about nothing is impossible.
Just so.
And it must, of course, also have a particular quality.
Of course.
So now, let's take note of ourselves.
Yes, we should.
Then I shall make a statement to you, putting things and actions together by means of a name and a verb. You should indicate to me what the statement is about.
Yes, just as far as I can.
"Theaetetus is sitting." Surely that is not a long statement?
No, it has just the right measure.
Now it is your turn to say what it is about, and to whom it refers.
Quite clear that it is about me, and refers to me.
Then what about this one?
What?
"Theaetetus, with whom I am conversing right now, is flying."
No one could deny that this too is mine, and refers to me.
And we maintain that each of these is necessarily of some quality.
Yes.
Now, what quality should we say each of these has?
One is false, the other true.
And the true one indicates the things that are, as they are, in your case.
Just so.
While the false one indicates things that are different from things that are.
Yes.
Then it speaks of things that are not, as if they are.
Just so.

But it speaks of things that are, though they are different from things that are about you. For we have said, you remember, that in the case of each, there are many things that are, and also many that are not.
Entirely so.
Now, the second statement I made about you, in the first place, based on the way we have defined statement, must necessarily be one of the shortest.
Well, that's how it was agreed just now anyway.
And, then, in turn, the statement must be about someone.
Yes.
And if it is not about you, surely it is not about anyone else.
Indeed not.
And it would not even be a statement at all if it were about no one. For we showed that it was impossible for there to be a statement which is a statement about nothing.
Quite right.

Then, in this statement about you, when different things are stated as the same and 'what is not' as 'what is', it appears that the combination of verbs with names absolutely turns out to be a real and true false statement.
Very true.
Now, what about thought, opinion and appearance? Isn't it already clear that all of these become both true and false in our souls?
How?
You will recognise this more easily if you first realise what each of these is, and how each differs from one another.
Just tell me.
Now, are not thought and speech the same, except that the silent dialogue of the soul with itself has been given the name 'thought'?
Quite so.
And the flow from the soul to the mouth which is vocally expressed has been given the name 'speech'.
True.
And what's more, we know that the following arises in speech.
What is that?
Affirmation and denial.
Yes, we know that.
So when this happens in the soul through thought, in silence, can you call it anything other than opinion?
What else?
What about this? Whenever such an experience arises in someone, not through himself but on account of perception, is there another appropriate name for this experience, except 'appearance'?
There is not.

Then, since speech turned out to be both true and false, and we showed that thought is the discourse of the soul with itself; and that opinion is the conclusion of thought; and what we mean by 'it appears' is a combination of perception and opinion; isn't it the case that any of these must be false sometimes since they are kindred to speech?
Of course.

Then do you appreciate that there has been an earlier discovery of false opinion and speech than was expected, when we feared that we were taking on an entirely impossible task by setting out in search of it?
I do.
Then we should not become disheartened by what remains. For since these have become apparent, we should recall the previous divisions on the basis of forms.
Which ones?
Well, we divided image-making into two forms: likeness-making and appearance-making.
Yes.
And we said that we were perplexed about which of these we would place the sophist in.
So we did.

And while we were unsure about this, even greater confusion arose for us, with the appearance of the argument which would dispute these, and maintain that there is no such thing as a likeness, image or appearance, since in no case at all is there any falsity, either in any way or at any time.
What you say is true.
But now, since false speech and false opinion have appeared, it is possible for there to be imitations of things that are, and from this disposition, a skill in deception arises.
Yes, it is possible.
And, indeed, we agreed earlier that the sophist was located in one of the divisions mentioned.
Yes.

Then let's try again, take the proposed kind and divide it in two, all the while proceeding to the right-hand part of what is being divided, holding on to the communion of the sophist, until we strip away whatever is common to the others, leaving only his own particular nature, which we shall display, first to ourselves, and then to those who are by nature most kindred to such a method.
Right.
Now, didn't we begin by dividing skill at that time into productive and acquisitive?
Yes.
And the sophist appeared to us in the acquisitive parts of hunting, contest, retailing, and certain kinds of that sort.
Yes, certainly.

But now, since he has been included under the skill of imitation, it is clear that we should first divide the productive skill in two. For presumably the skill of imitation is some kind of making, except that we shall say that it makes images, but not actual things. Is this so?
Yes, entirely so.
Now, in the first place, let there be two parts of the productive skill.
What are they?
The divine and the human.
I do not yet understand.
If you remember what was said at the start, we said that all production is the power which gives rise to whatever was not, previously.
We remember.

Now, with regard to all mortal animals, and as for all things that grow on earth from seeds and roots, and the lifeless bodies, with or without souls, that are formed within the earth: shall we say that some other than god is the producer who gives rise to them from non-being? Or are we to say what most people say and accept?
What?
That nature gives rise to them through some spontaneous cause that produces them without intelligence. Or are they produced with reasoning and divine knowledge that comes from god?

I myself, perhaps due to my age, often shift my views from one of these positions to the other. However, looking at you now, and noticing that you think that these things have arisen through divine agency, I myself also believe this is the case.

Good, Theaetetus, and if we thought that you were one of those people who would think differently in the future, we would now try, by means of an argument involving compelling persuasiveness, to make you agree. But since I am aware of your nature and recognise that even without our arguments, it is moving on by itself in the direction you say it is now inclined, I shall let the matter rest, for it would be a waste of time. Instead, let me propose that what are said to be the products of nature are produced by divine skill, while products that come from these products and are produced by humans, are produced by human skill. And, based on this account, there are two kinds of productive skill, the human and the divine.
Right.
Now, since there are two of these, divide each of them again in two.
How?
As though you were dividing the whole production skill widthwise just now, divide it lengthwise this time.
Take it as done.
In this way, there are now four parts in total: the two human parts on our side, and the two divine parts on the side of the gods.
Yes.

And, in turn, when divided in the other way, one part of each section is itself a making, while what remains in both cases is most accurately referred to as an image-making, and so production becomes two-fold again.
Tell me again how this division goes.

Well, presumably we ourselves, and the other animals, and the things from which natural objects come – fire, water and their kindred – we know that all of these are produced by the god, who has made each of them. Is this so?
Yes.
Following each of these, there are images, not the things themselves, and they have also come about through divine ingenuity.
What are they?

The phantoms that appear in dreams, and those that arise of their own accord during the day, such as a shadow when darkness occurs in firelight, and the doubles produced when one's own light, falling on bright and smooth surfaces, encounters the light from objects facing it, gives rise to an appearance opposite to the usual sight.
These two are, indeed, products of divine making: the actual object and the image which follows in each case.

What about our skill? Won't we say that on the one hand it produces the house itself by the skill of building, while on the other, by the skill of painting, it produces another, which is some sort of human-made dream for those who are awake.
Just so.

Then, on the same basis, all the other products of our productive activity also come in twos according to our account: there is the thing itself produced by the making skill, and the image produced by the image-making skill.

I understand better now. And I now propose that there are two twofold productive skills: the divine and the human, based on one division, and the other yields the things themselves and a sort of likeness of these.

Now let's recall that we said there are two forms of image-making: one is likeness-making, while the other is appearance-making, provided false had been shown to be truly false, and to belong by nature, among things that are.
Yes, it was so.
And this has appeared, and so on this basis shall we now propose, without dispute, that there are two forms?
Yes.
Then let's divide the appearance-making, in turn, in two.
How?
One is the appearance produced by instruments, while the other is when the maker of the appearance presents himself as the instrument.
What do you mean?
Whenever someone uses his own body or voice to make something appear like your body or your voice, I think this part of appearance-making is, in general, called imitation.
Yes.
Let us call this part imitation, and set it aside, and we shall be lazy and entrust the entire remainder to someone else, to make this one into one form and assign it an appropriate name.
Yes, that's how we should distinguish them and pass on the other.
And yet, Theaetetus, it is appropriate to think of this also as two-fold. Now consider the reason why.
Tell me.
Of those who imitate, some do so with knowledge of what they imitate, others without knowledge of it. And what distinction shall we make that is greater than that between knowledge and ignorance?
None.
Now, the imitation we just mentioned belonged to those who know. For someone who knows you and your character would imitate you.
Of course.

But what about the appearance of justice and excellence in general? Don't many, who are ignorant of these but somehow have some opinion about them, give the appearance of inhabiting them by being eager to imitate what they themselves think, in word and deed, as much as possible?
Yes, there are very many indeed.
So, do they all fail in seeming to be just, although they are not at all? Or is the opposite the case?
Quite the opposite.
I think then, we should say that this person is an imitator who is different from the other, the ignorant one from the one who knows.
Yes.

Now, where should we look for an appropriate name for each of them? Or is it obvious that this is somehow difficult, because there was some long-standing ignorance among the men of old when it came to dividing the kinds into forms, so that no one ever even bothered to make any division, and so it must be the case that names are not very abundant. However, even if it is somewhat rash to do so, let us, for the sake of the distinction, call the imitation based upon opinion, opinionative imitation, while the imitation based on knowledge is a kind of knowledgeable imitation.
Let it be so.
Well, we should use the former, for the sophist did not belong with those who know, but with those who imitate.
Yes, certainly.
Then let's examine this opinionative imitator, just like a piece of iron, to see whether he is sound or whether there is still some flaw in him.
We should examine him.

Indeed, there is a really very significant flaw. For one of them is naive, thinking that he knows the matters about which he holds opinions, while the disposition of the other has had a great deal of involvement in arguments, and his very disposition gives rise to misgivings and fears that he does not know what he pretends to know in the presence of others.
Yes, certainly. There are indeed both kinds you describe.
So, should we propose that one is a simple imitator while the other is an ironical imitator?
That's likely.
And should we, in turn, say that the form of this fellow is one, or two?
Consider it yourself.

I am considering it, and there appear, to a great extent, to be two. One I see, who is able to dissemble openly in lengthy speeches before large numbers, while the other does this in private, in short discourses, and forces the person who is conversing with him to contradict himself.
What you say is perfectly correct.
Now, who should we propose is the more long-winded type? Is he a statesman or a popular orator?
A popular orator.
And what shall we call the other? A wise person, or a sophist?

A wise person is impossible, since we proposed that he was ignorant, but since he is an imitator of a wise person, it is clear that he will have a name derived from his, and now I am almost in a position to recognise that we must really and truly refer to this person as the man who is sophist in every sense.
Then shall we put together his name, as we did before, weaving it together from end to beginning?
Quite so.

Now, the contradiction-making, ironical part of opinionative imitation belongs to the appearance-making kind, which is part of image-making and is marked off as the human, not the divine, part of production in the realm of word-making and wonder-working. So, anyone who says that the true sophist is "of that lineage and blood" will, it seems, speak the absolute truth.
Entirely so.
